A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CDVI research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across versions.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulated inference results in Table 2 and survival prediction experiments on seven clinical datasets in Tables 4–5.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds a posterior comparison in Figure 2 and experimental results in Appendix D.

M1.justification: The censor-dependent variational distribution, ELBO-C, CD-CVAE architecture, and IS and DVI estimators are retained. The shortened DVI label, parameter-sharing explanation and numerical implementation appendix do not establish a changed underlying method.

E1.justification: Both versions use SD1–SD6 and the same seven clinical datasets. Appendix D reuses SD3–SD5 and the existing clinical cohorts; it adds evaluations without introducing another population, domain or censoring scenario.

E2.justification: SAVAE, previously only discussed through Apellániz et al. (2024), is newly evaluated in Tables 7–10. The new simulated prediction comparison also includes the existing clinical baselines. The correction from DSF in v1’s prose to RSF does not introduce another comparator: v1 already reports RSF in its tables.

E3.justification: New Table 7 introduces held-out prediction evaluation on SD3–SD5, with exponential transformation of survival times, a 0.6/0.2/0.2 split and validation C-index selection. This supplements the retained simulation protocol that reports training inference gaps without validation or testing. Existing clinical splits and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Figure 2 compares learned and true posterior geometry on SD4 at x = 1, y = 0. Appendix D also quantifies the predictive effects of IS and DVI, supporting v1’s previously qualitative statement that these augmentations offer limited prediction improvements. No new robustness or distribution-shift regime is introduced.

E5.justification: V1 reports the best clinical test values across five repetitions without dispersion. V2 retains those summaries but adds five-run means and standard deviations throughout Tables 7–10. This substantially improves uncertainty reporting; it does not establish an increased run count for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: The numerical results in Tables 2, 4 and 5 are unchanged. New Tables 7–10 add simulated prediction results and clinical aggregate results, including SAVAE and augmentation variants; Figure 2 adds a qualitative posterior comparison. These are additional results, not demonstrated performance changes between versions under identical conditions.

T1.justification: Proposition 3.1 restricts its conclusions from all θ in Θ to θ in Θ_U, and Theorem 3.2.1 uses a volume-based density limit. Appendix C.5 adds a normalized-weight derivation of the DVI bias term. The principal theorems and proofs in Appendices A–B otherwise retain their mathematical substance.

C1.justification: The abstract and central CDVI contributions remain substantively unchanged. The rewritten introduction adds an explicit WHAS claim of '5% higher C-index'; new Table 8 reports 0.842 for CD-CVAE versus 0.791 for the strongest external comparator, RSF.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly frames the support-overlap argument in the infinite-data limit and softens the benchmark conclusion from vanilla VI being 'at least suboptimal' to 'can be suboptimal.' It also explains the dependence between the event and censoring variational parameters. Existing interpretations of amortization effects and limited augmentation benefits remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix C.5 documents normalized weights and LogSumExp computation for the existing DVI correction, while Section 3.2.2 clarifies joint network parameterization. Software, hardware requirements, hyperparameter ranges and code access in the retained material are unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 expands supporting citations and the existing VI discussion to include inverse autoregressive flows, alternative divergences, disentanglement and label-aware VAEs. It also adds references on censoring and evaluation. The three-part positioning of its contributions and its central criticism of earlier survival VI remain intact.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten around explicit contributions, and the preliminary and theoretical explanations are extensively revised. Section 3 gains subdivisions separating the edge case, censoring assumptions, posterior optimality and ELBO construction. New computational and experimental appendices further reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: V2 adds the posterior contour comparison in Figure 2 and four experimental tables with uncertainty displays in Appendix D. Figure 1 gains colored structural distinctions, and the encoder diagram is revised. These substantially expand the visual presentation beyond the relocation and renumbering of retained material.

improvement.justification: SAVAE comparisons, held-out simulations and mean ± standard deviation tables make v1’s best-run-only evidence easier to assess; clearer exposition and the corrected scope of Proposition 3.1 also help. Gains are tempered by unresolved reporting issues: Table 8’s DSM SUPPORT mean, 0.668, exceeds Table 4’s stated maximum, 0.666, without explaining differing runs or settings. Appendix C.5 also omits the required squared weights in its final computational instruction.
